title: E49 - Harvey and Legora vs AI First Firms, Logan Brown, Soxton
author: Logan Brown

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: The source shifts attention from AI-enabled in-house insourcing to an AI-first external service that can substitute for, or delay, internal legal hiring among startups. It nevertheless preserves the cluster’s selective rather than universal framing by limiting that substitution to automatable, routine work and directing complex matters elsewhere.
qs: We have Series B clients that have told us that Soxton is allowing them to delay getting a GC.
So if people come to me with things that are very complex, like if you have a nasty down round where you're cramming people down, it might not be a Soxton job for us.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source anticipates automation of suitable legal work and continued lawyer review, aligning with the cluster’s delivery and pricing implications. However, it does not address whether automation erodes junior apprenticeship, creates a verification-expertise paradox, or requires reconstructed training, so its position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.
qs: But I do think that, like, the things that should be automated will be, and there's going to be somebody doing that.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source addresses lawyers’ growing engagement with AI and the association between use and favourable sentiment, but it does not assess access-to-justice outcomes, service transformation, or whether adoption can close the justice gap. Its evidence therefore does not establish a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: And so I think that it is definitely becoming on folks' radar more.
And what the survey found overwhelmingly is, when you use AI more, you like it more.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts the need to rebuild legal delivery around client needs rather than merely add AI to inherited hourly workflows, and materially extends the cluster with Soxton’s concrete AI-first model: per-contract pricing, AI-enabled production and lawyer review. It also reinforces the cluster’s competition, access and evidentiary-caution themes, while offering little on apprenticeship or staffing succession.
qs: I'm, like, okay, from the ground up, what is the best way to get this, like, work to a customer?

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Soxton accepts the cluster’s core model of bounded, AI-enabled legal delivery backed by specialist lawyers, and adds a concrete operating rule: undertake only automatable work where AI adds value and internal subject-matter expertise exists. It also extends the commercial thesis by suggesting AI-first external services may defer some startups’ need for an in-house GC, though that remains a prediction.
qs: I'm only interested in doing the things that are automatable and where AI is a real value added.
And if we don't have that expertise there, we won't do it.

st.t: Repeatable services: Organisational redesign changes legal delivery
st.an: Brown accepts the cluster’s central proposition that AI requires organisational and business-model redesign, not merely software-assisted lawyers. Soxton concretely extends it through ground-up customer-focused delivery, per-contract pricing, lawyer review and adaptive quality control, while predicting coexistence with specialist Big Law rather than wholesale replacement.
qs: But I think that, like, my decision to leave is, I think half of what needs to be disrupted here is the business model.
I'm, like, okay, from the ground up, what is the best way to get this, like, work to a customer?

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Soxton accepts the cluster’s core proposition and supplies a concrete AI-native service model: fixed-fee delivery, agents performing bounded first-pass work, and experienced lawyers reviewing output. Brown also limits automation to suitable work and predicts restructuring rather than lawyers’ disappearance, though her evidence is primarily company-reported operating experience rather than independent validation.
qs: But I think that, like, my decision to leave is, I think half of what needs to be disrupted here is the business model.
And then a team of lawyers will review it before it goes back to the client.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Brown accepts that AI will automate suitable legal tasks while lawyers and established firms retain specialized advisory roles. He materially extends the cluster by arguing that realizing this shift requires redesigning delivery and pricing—not merely adding AI to traditional practice—and illustrates that model with fixed per-contract pricing and lawyer review.
qs: But I think that, like, my decision to leave is, I think half of what needs to be disrupted here is the business model.
But I do think that, like, the things that should be automated will be, and there's going to be somebody doing that.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that AI selectively automates suitable work while humans remain important, and materially extends it with an AI-first legal-service model built around first-principles workflow and pricing redesign. It also proposes agent-based checks as an operational response to errors, though its broader market effects remain predictions rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: I'm, like, okay, from the ground up, what is the best way to get this, like, work to a customer?
And you make a mistake in Soxton, if it's something with client work, we can spin up an agent or two agents that will double check everything going forward in the future.

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: Brown supports the cluster’s conditional optimism by predicting that AI will remove fear-inducing, draining tasks while preserving lawyers’ intellectual work. Her claim aligns with preparing for beneficial change without proving transformation, because it is qualitative and unaccompanied by measured outcomes.
qs: And so I also think that being a lawyer will be a better job because the parts that induce fear, the parts that just are soul-sucking, they're going away.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s nuanced account of resistance by rejecting the claim that individual lawyers deliberately slow work to increase fees, while leaving competition between incumbent AI vendors and AI-native firms unresolved. It reinforces two cluster qualifications but does not materially extend the organisational-redesign thesis.
qs: I don't remember ever doing anything at a law firm as a junior associate, where it did not feel like there was someone waiting outside the office, like, get it done right now, fast, move, move, move, move.

st.t: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s framing that legal AI’s strategic significance extends beyond tool adoption to changes in business models and competitive structure. It highlights varied technology choices and the possible emergence of AI-first firms, while presenting lawyer departures and improved working conditions as expectations rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: But they're not spending enough time focusing on, what are we going to need to do as a business because AI exists in the world?

And one of the best examples I've been highlighting in recent years is firms need to be aware that once their top lawyers start using AI, they may come to the conclusion that, you know what, I don't necessarily need this big law firm anymore.

kp.k: AI adoption can catalyse departures from established firms
kp.d: Host Zach Abramowitz argues that firms must consider business consequences of AI, not just tools, use cases and adoption: lawyers may conclude that AI makes independent practices more attractive and lucrative. He describes a quiet exodus into boutiques without providing counts. Logan Brown's account supplies an individual example: after using Harvey at Cooley, she left in May 2025 and built Soxton around a different delivery model.
qs: Too many firms think about how they should be using AI. Not enough firms think about what they need to be doing because AI.
if I have this, why do I need this firm?
I left Cooley in May of last year. It's like 2025 and the models have improved so much

kp.k: Soxton combines agent drafting with mandatory lawyer review
kp.d: Brown describes Soxton as an outside AI-powered general counsel service for early-stage startups. Agents take the first step on work previously performed manually, and lawyers review it before client delivery. She reports pricing of $100 a contract. This is an account of AI-assisted service delivery, not software sales or autonomous legal advice; the transcript provides no independent productivity or accuracy measurements.
qs: We position ourselves as an outside AI powered GC for early stage startups.
Now we have a suite of agents take first step at that. And then a team of lawyers will review it before it goes back to the client.
It's $100 a contract.

kp.k: Automation suitability and expertise constrain service scope
kp.d: Brown says Soxton focuses on automatable matters and refers complex or unsupported work elsewhere, including potentially contentious down rounds. She reports over 40 attorneys, each with at least five years of relevant Big Law experience, and says half its customers also engage established firms. Soxton had recently completed a few seed financings; Brown considers some financing work suitable for conventional automation without AI. These are founder-reported operating details, not comparative results.
qs: half of our customers are also engaged in a Cooley, Wilson, Finwick, Perkins type of place.
I'm only interested in doing the things that are automatable and where AI is a real value added.
I have about 40, over 40 attorneys working for me, and everybody has worked in big law at one of these places for at least five years with a lot of experience in a specific field.
And if we don't have that expertise there, we won't do it.
there's so much that could have just been done previously just using automations or we don't even need the AI part of it since it's a routine.

kp.k: Outsourced advice may delay in-house general counsel hiring
kp.d: Brown reports that Series B clients say Soxton lets them postpone hiring a GC, using it up to five times daily for routine questions. She describes $50 chats with a response within four hours. In her assessment, substantial administrative coordination or highly regulated operations remain triggers for in-house hiring; she explicitly declines to predict the threshold five years ahead because regulation and tooling may change.
qs: We have Series B clients that have told us that Soxton is allowing them to delay getting a GC.
They'll use us five times a day for quick gut checks and just managing those day-to-day questions
they can have access to like $50 a chat.
So you can just ask a lawyer a question, and we'll get back to you within four hours.
Or if you're in like a highly regulated field, where you're going to be managing a lot of regulators and administrative licenses, that seems to be the threshold now.

kp.k: Lower prices target previously unserved entrepreneurs
kp.d: Brown frames market expansion as serving founders who otherwise would not obtain a lawyer or would rely on ChatGPT. She describes customers ranging from Series B companies to people building businesses outside working hours. Her growth thesis is a prediction that falling entrepreneurship costs will expand business formation and legal demand over the next 5, 10 and 15 years, not a measured market forecast.
qs: Like folks that otherwise wouldn't use a lawyer or would just use ChatGPT and allowing greater access to excellent legal services is our goal.
I think that the price of entrepreneurship has never been lower.
I don't think that like starting companies is the only thing Soxton is going to do ever, but it is like where we've chosen to start.
something that I think will continue to be fruitful in the next 5, 10, 15 years.

kp.k: Venture financing is optional, but supports Brown's scale ambitions
kp.d: Brown distinguishes bootstrapped AI-first solo practices from venture-backed providers. She says her venture route reflects her access-to-justice and scale objectives rather than a universal financing requirement. She expects a heterogeneous market, from small practices to larger businesses and providers handling major private-equity transactions. The discussion does not specify Soxton's financing amount or ownership arrangements.
qs: I think you could absolutely build an AI first law firm and like solo shop and like grow in the traditional way without needing VC money.
I have chosen pick the venture route, and I'm doing that because I'm largely focused on like an access to justice, like I really need to get to scale
It's just like a new way to practice law. So it will be the solo shops, but then they'll also be like the bigger, bigger folks.

kp.k: Business-model redesign matters alongside AI tooling
kp.d: Brown argues that applying AI within the existing partnership model is distinct from rebuilding service delivery around automation and fixed prices. She considers partner-income maximisation incompatible with her own access goals. She predicts coexistence: automation-oriented providers will handle suitable tasks while established firms survive and may charge higher hourly rates for specialised advice. These are strategic judgments and forecasts rather than demonstrated market outcomes.
qs: I think half of what needs to be disrupted here is the business model.
I think that many big law firms will still exist. I think the billable hour rate will go up for, like, those highly specialized advisory work
we're, like, anti-billable hour here.
my goal, which is I want more people to have access to high-quality like legal, that's just different and adverse to having a partnership that is trying to maximize the amount that partners make.

kp.k: More complexity and entrepreneurship could expand legal demand
kp.d: Abramowitz predicts continued demand for human support on deals above $50 million, more lawyers and higher rates, as well as litigation against rapidly expanding AI companies. Brown separately anticipates litigation over applying existing and new laws to AI, alongside more deals and acquisitions as companies proliferate. Neither speaker supplies labour-market estimates or quantified demand evidence.
qs: as long as there are deals that are valued at above $50 million, I guarantee you someone is going to want a human being holding their hand on that for the foreseeable future.
To me, I think there's going to be more lawyers, higher rates, a lot of this stuff.
The laws are not caught up to what AI is doing, and so we'll have to figure all of this out
I think that we're going to see more deals, there's going to be more companies being started, more acquisitions.

kp.k: Easier claim generation may intensify court backlogs
kp.d: Brown predicts that easier access to filing and agents searching for potential plaintiffs' claims will transform litigation, while courts' slow internal AI adoption worsens backlogs. Abramowitz asserts that AI-generated suits already exceed court bandwidth and argues AI will also be needed to manage the burden, referencing prior podcast guests rather than supplying court data. The discussion separates expanded access to remedies from institutions' capacity to process claims.
qs: I think small claims courts and court systems are going to be in for a world of change, and I also think that those will be the last folks to adopt AI internally
I think we'll see a backlog of court systems and litigation I think will be really fruitful.
AI-generated lawsuits are already pressing the court beyond bandwidth.
the number of agents that are going to be crawling for plaintiff's lawsuits and people in their day-to-day, that can suddenly file a lawsuit because they've been wronged.

kp.k: Growing adoption coexists with professional resistance
kp.d: Brown reports heightened lawyer engagement with AI over the last six and three months, increased hostile emails following Soxton's December emergence from stealth, and job applications. Abramowitz cites a Law360 survey released the prior year linking greater use to more positive sentiment, but provides no sample, percentages or methodology. His expectation that users remain favourable and both speakers' impressions of online sentiment are not representative population findings.
qs: Last six months, last three months, I think that the bar and its concern for technology is just rapidly transforming.
we came out of stealth in December.
I get a lot of emails from folks that are just concerned, but also a lot of people applying for jobs.
Law 360 released a survey last year in which they asked lawyers about their sentiment towards AI.
when you use AI more, you like it more. If you don't use AI, you tend not to like it.

kp.k: Hallucination incidents prompt verification and proportionality debates
kp.d: Discussing a reported Sullivan and Cromwell filing incident, both speakers oppose personal vilification. Brown speculates about fatigue and missed checks; Abramowitz speculates about version control while acknowledging uncertainty. Brown expects further mistakes and review layers, comparing the transition with early Westlaw adoption. Abramowitz questions sanctions and offers an unsupported heuristic of 500 non-hallucination cases per detected case as an adoption indicator; it is not a measured error rate. His additional point is that urgent practice conditions complicate claims that hourly lawyers deliberately work slowly.
qs: I don't know exactly what happened in this case
My guess is that's probably what happened here without fully knowing it.
assume that for every case that's got like hallucinations in it, there's probably 500 that don't.
This is a mistake. It sucks. I hope they don't do it again, but I don't think it's a moral failing.
there are so many different layers of review that happened before this gets filed. And I'm sure that there will be more in the future in response to this.
There's this impression that lawyers are literally dragging their feet at firms to work slowly so that they can charge more.

kp.k: Legal-AI incumbency depends on workflows, not merely distribution
kp.d: Brown reports that most associate friends use Harvey or Legora as a default starting point and credits vendors' partner-facing distribution. Her product comparison is secondhand: she has not used Legora, and notes that model improvements can be mistaken for product superiority. She questions staying power if Claude Enterprise performs better before vendors establish integrated workflows. Soxton itself uses existing models with proprietary technology rather than either vendor.
qs: So I haven't used Legora.
We don't use either in Soxton where like we have our, we use the existing models and we have our own proprietary tech on top of that.
most of my friends that are associates have switched over to having Harvey or Legora be their default

if like Claude Enterprise is able to get into these firms and it works slightly better and there hasn't been able, like an entire workflow regime that these companies have built out, that's where I don't know where the staying power is.
My friends seem to prefer Legora, but it seems to be neck and neck.

kp.k: Application vendors face foundation-model and specialised workflow competition
kp.d: Abramowitz questions how application-layer valuations will be sustained against Claude, demand for bespoke firm systems and vendors designing workflows specifically for in-house teams. He discloses investment in Sandstone. Both speakers counterbalance skepticism with respect for Harvey's and Legora's execution and uncertainty about their plans. Brown distinguishes law-firm software, in-house software, AI-first service delivery and back-office tools, predicting increasingly blurred boundaries; her taxonomy explicitly excludes litigation.
qs: it's really hard to understand the application layer companies and how they're going to continue justifying these valuations
I'm invested in Sandstone
they are building in-house workflows that are specially designed for those teams.
these teams have really executed.
then you have like my realm of like AI first law firms, where we're delivering the services and then like the back office work, the timekeeping, and this doesn't include litigation.
I think that you'll just see like those lines be blurred all up and down the stack.

kp.k: Brand visibility may promote use after enterprise purchasing
kp.d: In discussing legal-AI marketing strategy, Brown initially questions whether broad advertising influences firm purchasing. Abramowitz hypothesises that familiarity and shared exposure can increase individual lawyers' use after a firm has already purchased the product, rather than merely generate sales. Brown finds the mechanism plausible. Neither provides adoption data or evidence of campaign effectiveness.
qs: I don't know the effectiveness of it.
this is not just about like getting in the door in terms of like selling to firms. I actually think it's about increasing adoption.
I think that what we're seeing is that NPS and brand familiarity actually is a part of like the adoption circuit.

kp.k: Firms may need stronger engineering recruitment capabilities
kp.d: Abramowitz argues that law firms lack a culture of paying for senior developers and have not adequately presented themselves as attractive technology workplaces. Drawing on his own recruitment assistance, he predicts this must change. His broader analogy is that developer employment could spread beyond technology companies into conventional businesses; no hiring or compensation figures are supplied.
qs: law firms do not have a culture of paying for top senior developers
they haven't really done a very good job of saying like, hey, it's cool to come work at a law firm.
I've helped law firms recruit top senior talent

kp.k: AI-first management promises different quality controls and work experiences
kp.d: Brown says Soxton can respond to client-work errors by deploying additional checking agents, and characterises its quality control as excellent without measured validation. She argues this can reduce the fear and tedious work associated with Big Law and leave lawyers focused on thinking. This claimed automated checking supplements her earlier account of human review; it does not demonstrate that human verification is unnecessary.
qs: you make a mistake in Soxton, if it's something with client work, we can spin up an agent or two agents that will double check everything going forward in the future.
Our quality control is excellent.
I also think that being a lawyer will be a better job because the parts that induce fear, the parts that just are soul-sucking, they're going away. It's like the thinking part that's remaining.

kp.k: Radical market change remains an explicitly uncertain forecast
kp.d: Brown predicts an unrecognisable legal landscape in five and 10 years, attributing change to capital, capable entrepreneurs and pressure to adopt technology. She uses the Yellow Pages-to-search transition as an analogy, not empirical evidence. When Abramowitz suggests firms may disappear or become skeletons, she emphasises that many will survive and that specific outcomes remain hypotheses.
qs: I think that many still exist and are able to survive it.
I do think that the legal landscape will be unrecognizable in five and 10 years.
There's so much money being poured into legal tech, and there are so many capable entrepreneurs that are using it to change the way that it works
So I have guesses and hypotheses about some of the things that change and what it looks like, but I don't think that we know.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Logan Brown describes AI-first legal services as a different delivery and business model, and predicts expanded legal demand, changing competition, and a substantially transformed profession.
pts.d: Brown says Soxton supplies outside-GC services to early-stage startups using agents for initial work and lawyers for human verification, charging $100 per contract rather than billing by the hour (00:04:08; 00:29:27). Its intended market includes founders who otherwise would not hire a lawyer or would use ChatGPT alone. She reports that some Series B clients use Soxton to delay hiring an in-house GC (00:07:48). She argues that changing the business model matters alongside adopting AI tools: automatable work will be automated, while many Big Law firms will survive and charge higher hourly rates for highly specialized advice (00:29:27). She expects AI-first firms to range from solo practices to larger businesses, with venture funding optional rather than intrinsic to the model (00:12:12). She predicts more companies, deals, acquisitions, and litigation, including disputes about AI and easier access to filing claims; slower court adoption could produce backlogs, while AI will also transform dispute management (00:14:52–00:16:58). She expects additional AI-related legal-research mistakes during the technology transition (00:25:54). For legal-AI vendors, she describes Harvey and Legora as embedded in associates' workflows but questions their durability if general-purpose competitors outperform them without a defensible workflow offering (00:32:29). She anticipates blurred boundaries between law-firm software, in-house software, AI-first service delivery, and back-office tooling (00:41:19). She predicts a legal landscape unrecognizable in five to ten years and better outcomes for consumers, while acknowledging uncertainty about its exact form (00:42:24). Finally, she says AI-assisted checking and removal of unpleasant routine work can improve lawyers' working lives and leave more of the thinking work (00:44:27). These are Brown's claims; the host's independent forecasts are not attributed to her.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Brown primarily offers operational experience, client reports, peer anecdotes, and historical analogy rather than systematic measurements.
pts.d: Her account of Soxton draws on her experience doing startup work at Cooley for almost three years and running the new firm. She supplies service prices, reports a few completed financing transactions, says roughly half of customers also engage established law firms, and reports over 40 attorneys with substantial Big Law experience (00:04:08–00:07:48). Client statements support the reported delay in hiring GCs, but the transcript supplies no independent assessment of cost savings, service quality, or the prevalence of that effect. Her claim that quality control is excellent is a founder's assessment, accompanied by an example of deploying agents to check for recurring errors, not a measured error-rate comparison (00:44:27). Her observations about Harvey and Legora rely substantially on friends' accounts and group chats. She used Harvey at Cooley, left in May 2025, has not used Legora, and says model improvements limit comparisons with her earlier experience; Soxton uses underlying models with proprietary technology rather than either product (00:31:14–00:33:47). Her expectation of transitional research mistakes invokes accounts of concerns during the adoption of Westlaw and internet research (00:25:54), not model benchmarking. Discussion of a recent filing error does not establish its cause: her explanations involving fatigue, missed checks, or version control are explicitly conjectural. Her broader predictions about litigation growth, higher specialist rates, court adoption, industry restructuring, and improved working lives are reasoned forecasts rather than findings established by quantitative evidence in this interview.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Brown distinguishes current service capabilities from conditional vendor forecasts and uncertain five-to-ten-year industry change.
pts.d: The current-service claims concern the interview period in the document labeled 2026. Brown says she left Cooley in May 2025, describes Soxton as new, and says it has only recently begun handling seed financings. Its present scope is restricted to work where automation adds value and the firm has relevant expertise; complex matters such as a contentious down round may go elsewhere (00:05:09–00:06:11). Lawyer review remains part of delivery, so this is not a claim of autonomous legal advice. Startup demand is a bet she expects to remain fruitful over five, ten, and fifteen years (00:13:19). Venture funding is her choice to pursue scale and access goals, not a requirement for all AI-first practices (00:12:12). The current threshold for hiring a GC includes substantial administrative coordination or highly regulated operations; she declines to specify the threshold five years ahead because regulation and tooling may change (00:07:48). Her prediction of higher Big Law rates concerns highly specialized advisory work, not every service. Her doubts about Harvey and Legora are conditional on Claude Enterprise entering firms, working better, and the specialist vendors lacking sufficiently developed workflows (00:32:29). She forecasts major legal-market change over five and ten years but explicitly allows that many incumbent firms survive and that the eventual structure is unknown (00:42:24). Litigation growth, court backlogs, further research mistakes, and better lawyer working lives have no precise numerical timetable.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects span underserved founders, startup legal departments, incumbent and AI-first providers, software vendors, lawyers, courts, and consumers.
pts.d: For early-stage founders and small businesses that would otherwise forgo legal help, Brown presents lower-priced lawyer-reviewed services as an expansion of access; this is distinct from her claim that established Series B clients can reduce overhead and postpone an in-house GC hire. She reports $50 lawyer chats with a response within four hours for day-to-day questions (00:07:48). Established law firms may retain complex and specialized matters while facing competition for automatable work; the fact that many Soxton customers also use Big Law illustrates complementary as well as competitive relationships (00:06:11; 00:29:27). Lawyers can form solo or larger AI-first practices, and Brown expects their jobs to shift away from routine, fear-inducing tasks toward thinking. Deal lawyers and litigators could receive more work from entrepreneurship, acquisitions, AI-related disputes, and easier claims initiation (00:14:52). Courts, particularly small-claims systems, may face more filings before adopting sufficient internal AI capacity. Harvey and Legora are software vendors, whereas Brown describes Soxton's category as delivering legal services; in-house teams are buyers of a separate but overlapping tooling market (00:41:19). She predicts competition and convergence across these categories, rather than demonstrating that one model will eliminate the others. Her overall consumer-benefit prediction is broad and expressly uncertain as to the eventual market structure.
